title: Beautiful Ghibli diorama kits lets you build anime characters’ homes inside yours [Photos]
description: Papercraft models are small in size, but colossally cool for fans of Studio Ghibli. Earlier in the year Ghibli Park added a new exhibit consisting of over 30 large dioramas made by famed anime director Hayao Miyazaki. Odds are, though, that you don’t have that much space to devote to your love of Ghibli’s art […]
content:
Papercraft models are small in size, but colossally cool for fans of Studio Ghibli.

Earlier in the year Ghibli Park added a new exhibit consisting of over 30 large dioramas made by famed anime director Hayao Miyazaki. Odds are, though, that you don’t have that much space to devote to your love of Ghibli’s art and environments, but Japanese papercraft company Sankei does have a way to let you bring a little piece of the Ghibli world into your home.

Going on sale November 3 are three new entries in Sankei’s Miniatuart Mini Plus line, recreating locations from Howl’s Moving Castle, Kiki’s Delivery Service, and Arrietty.

Each of them starts as a box filled with sheets of paper from which to build the walls and interior, and after you assemble everything the box then becomes a stand for the completed diorama.

Though the scale is compact and the building materials simple, the kits contain an incredible level of charming detail. Howl’s hearth, for example, is cluttered with all sorts of magical baubles and reference materials, just as you’d expect the eccentric wizard’s living quarters to be, and even fire spirit Calcifer makes an appearance.

The room that Kiki and Jiji rent from bakery owner Osono is decidedly less chaotic, but still has a lived-in feel with the witch’s laundry hanging up to dry, her broom leaning against the windowsill, and Jiji making sure not to leave any dirty pawprints on the nice clean floor.

The Kiki’s kit also has the most detailed exterior, which really helps create the atmosphere of it being a miniaturized loft that scaled-down version of the characters could live inside.

▼ The kits’ boxes/bases bear different illustrations on different sides, too, giving you one more reason to view them from different angles

Rounding out the trio is Arietty’s family’s living room.

This one comes with an extra dash of coolness because the scale of the diorama (6 centimeters [2.4 inches] square) works as a reminder that Arietty and her kin are all so tiny that most of the humans whose house they lived inside of never noticed them.

All of the locations are filled with cozy vibes, but they are listed on Sankei’s website as being advanced-difficulty kits, with an estimated time of five hours or more to build Kiki’s room, and 10 hours or more for the others. Kiki’s kit is also the lowest-priced of the bunch at 4,290 yen (US$27), followed by Arrietty’s (6,160 yen) and Howl’s (6,600 yen). All three can be ordered starting November 3 through Sankei’s Rakuten online storefront (here, here, and here).

Source: Sankei

title: Pokémon guitars from Fender Japan come with 8-bit sound mode for covering retro game music [Vid]
description: Fender celebrates Red and Green’s 30th anniversary with guitars saluting the Pokémon world in both looks and sound. In the English-speaking world, the start of the Pokémon video game series were the paired releases of Pokémon Red and Blue for the Game Boy in 1998. However, unbeknownst to many young fans at the time, the […]
content:
Fender celebrates Red and Green’s 30th anniversary with guitars saluting the Pokémon world in both looks and sound.

In the English-speaking world, the start of the Pokémon video game series were the paired releases of Pokémon Red and Blue for the Game Boy in 1998. However, unbeknownst to many young fans at the time, the real origins of the franchise had come out in Japan two years prior, and were titled Pokémon Red and Green.

Here in 2026, the global Poké-fan community has a more comprehensive picture of the franchise’s history, which brings us to the appropriate color schemes for the latest collaboration celebrating Pokémon’s 30th anniversary, a pair of customized guitars created in partnership with Fender Japan.

In a parallel to how mainline Pokémon games customarily have a similar but still different sibling, so too has Fender chosen two different models of guitar for this team-up, the Made in Japan Pokémon “Red Version” Stratocaster and Made in Japan Pokémon “Green Version” Telecaster.

Within the series’ visual design language, the color red is often associated with Fire-type Pocket Monsters, and green with Grass-types, so the body of each guitar is covered in pixel art of species from those categories.

More fan-service flair can be found on the neck, where Poké Balls are subtly scattered about…

…and the backside features a Pokémon 30th anniversary plate.

In addition to their visual salutes to the Pokémon world, these made-in-Japan guitars make an audio one too.

Push in the volume knob, and you can activate what Fender has dubbed the instruments’ “8-Bit Sound System Mode,” a clever audio effect that gives the guitar’s sound a quality reminiscent of nostalgic chiptunes, which should lend itself really well to playing covers of classic Pokémon games’ soundtracks.

▼ A demonstration video of the 8-Bit Sound System Mode

楽器メーカーFender®とコラボした『ポケットモンスター 赤・緑』デザインのギターが、ポケモンセンターオンラインに登場！
11月19日（木）、12時から抽選販売の応募が開始されるよ。
音色に8-bitサウンドが加わるギミックも搭載！
ぜひ動画で聴いてみてね。https://t.co/c6Xlr0hX3H #ポケモンセンター pic.twitter.com/ydajspcaQ0

— ポケモン公式 (@Pokemon_cojp) October 30, 2026

Each guitar also comes bundled with a selection of pixel art picks, plus a custom hardcase and certificate of authenticity.

Because they’ll be available in limited quantities, both guitars, priced at 396,000 yen (US$2,490) each, will be offered for sale through a lottery system from the Pokémon Center Online store, which will be accepting applications between noon on November 19 and 4:59 p.m. on November 24 (Japan time).

Related: Pokémon Center Online

title: This semi-secret, totally free footbath in downtown Tokyo is completely awesome
description: The Museum of Narratives has an oasis for your feet. They say there’s no such thing as a free lunch, but it turns out there is a free foot bath in Tokyo. It’s not some rinky-dink little tub in some obscure spot on the outskirts of the capital, either, but right in the middle of […]
content:
The Museum of Narratives has an oasis for your feet.

They say there’s no such thing as a free lunch, but it turns out there is a free foot bath in Tokyo. It’s not some rinky-dink little tub in some obscure spot on the outskirts of the capital, either, but right in the middle of downtown, near Takanawa Gateway Station on the Yamanote train line that encircles the city center.

Takanawa Gateway is the newest station on the line, and is connected to a shopping, entertainment, and cultural development called Takanawa Gateway City, part of which is MoN Takanawa: The Museum of Narratives.

The museum, which opened in March, hosts rotating artistic and cultural events, but on our visit, we didn’t need to purchase a ticket, because we weren’t heading inside the main exhibition areas. Instead, our destination was someplace on the sixth-floor, an exterior area that many people aren’t aware of called the Ashiyu Terrace. Ashiyu is the Japanese word for “footbath,” and that’s exactly what you’ll find here!

This outdoor urban oasis has an outer ring of greenery, and beyond that offers impressively open views of the surrounding cityscape, of a kind that’s not easy to come by this deep in downtown without going to a skyscraper’s upper floors.

This is thanks to the terrace’s position adjacent to the train tracks, plus Takanawa Gateway’s proximity to the next station to the south, Shinagawa. Shinagawa is one of Japan’s densest rail hubs, and the seven different lines that converge there each need their own amount of space as they approach the station, creating a rare broad, low patch in downtown Tokyo’s urban topography that creates wide lines of sight.

▼ This also makes the MoN Takanawa footbath a great place for trainspotting rail fans.

Because the foot bath is open-air, it’s probably not the most pleasant place to spend a blisteringly hot summer day or a frigidly cold winter evening. Right now, though, on a fall afternoon, the weather is perfect for this sort of thing, especially since in addition to a cozy-warm hot water area…

…the Ashiyu Terrace also has a cold water area.

This means you can start off in the warm section until you’re feeling nice and toasty, and once you get a little too hot, you can mosey on over to the other end of the bath and cool down. Then, if you’re anything like us, you’ll eventually migrate back to the warm section, and repeat the process a couple more times before you’re ready to leave this ankle-deep aquatic paradise.

If you’re looking for more ways to enjoy traditional Japanese culture on the free-to-access museum grounds, there’s a little Shinto shrine on the rooftop…

…and a tatami reed-floor relaxation room on the fourth floor with digital art displays, which is also free to access.

▼ The tatami mats are new enough that they still have a very noticeable relaxing earthy fragrance.

Really, the only possibly negative thing we could say about the Ashiyu Terrace is that no towels are provided, but we’re happy to bring our own handkerchief to dry off with when the rest of this experience is this awesome.

Location information
MoN Takanawa: The Museum of Narratives
Adress: Tokyo-to, Minato-ku, Mita 3-16-6
Open 10 a.m.-9 p.m.
Website

title: Japan’s TeamLab digital art group is opening a permanent museum in America
description: Internationally acclaimed art collective will have a new home not far from Disneyland. Japan’s TeamLab has risen from relative obscurity to become one of the most admired digital art collectives in the world, using their technological wizardry and ethereally emotional sensibilities to craft experiences unlike those from anyone else. Their exhibits and museums regularly top […]
content:
Internationally acclaimed art collective will have a new home not far from Disneyland.

Japan’s TeamLab has risen from relative obscurity to become one of the most admired digital art collectives in the world, using their technological wizardry and ethereally emotional sensibilities to craft experiences unlike those from anyone else. Their exhibits and museums regularly top lists of must-visit places for artistically inclined travelers in Japan, but now it’s time for TeamLab itself to embark on an overseas journey, as it’s announced that it will be opening its very first permanent museum in the U.S.

Sunny southern California is where TeamLab will be setting up in the States. The group’s facility will be part of the city of Anaheim’s currently in-development OCVIBE cultural, entertainment, and sports complex, which will also have green spaces, offices, hotels, and apartments.

▼ Examples of the sort of art that TeamLab creates

TeamLab Museum Anaheim is the tentative name of the facility, but it won’t be a shock if they eventually decide on something with a little more pizazz, seeing as how their museums in Japan have creative names such as TeamLab Borderless or TeamLab Planets. The Anaheim museum is planned to have a total floor space of roughly 10,000 square meters (approximately 110,000 square feet).

▼ A preview image showing TeamLab Museum Anaheim, with its shimmery sea green exterior, connected by a pedestrian bridge to the Anaheim Regional Transportation Intermodal Center rail station, with Angel Stadium behind it on the opposite side of the 57 Freeway

In announcing the Anaheim museum, TeamLab co-founder and director Toshiyuki Inoko said:

“I am filled with happiness that we will be opening TeamLab’s first large-scale museum in America at OCVIBE in Anaheim. Through art, TeamLab seeks to explore the nature of consciousness and existence. Our exhibits change through the existence of people, with visitors themselves becoming part of the piece. By becoming immersed in the artwork, visitors are connected, without boundaries, to both the installation and the world. By gathering and placing ourselves alongside others in this location where sports, music, and culture intersect, we will come to perceive the world in new ways and share those perceptions with others.”

OCVIBE is planned to open in phases, with the first coming in the spring of next year and featuring an amphitheater, restaurants, and park. TeamLab’s museum, though, is projected to open in 2030, but fans will tell you that the group’s creations are worth the wait, and that’s still two years earlier than the projected opening of its new Tokyo museum.

title: Can Japan’s Self-Defense Forces legally open fire on a zombie horde?
description: This legal discussion contains scenes of explicit violence and gore. It’s Halloween again, and what better way to ring in the spookiest of holidays than with some thought exercises on complex constitutional law issues. Although most zombie stories focus on a ragtag group of civilians coping with civilization collapsing all around them, the beginning of […]
content:
This legal discussion contains scenes of explicit violence and gore.

It’s Halloween again, and what better way to ring in the spookiest of holidays than with some thought exercises on complex constitutional law issues. Although most zombie stories focus on a ragtag group of civilians coping with civilization collapsing all around them, the beginning of the outbreak usually shows the military going all out in trying to eliminate the undead threat.

And with many of these movies and TV shows taking place in the USA, it’s no surprise to see the armed forces meeting the waves of zombies with guns blazing. In Japan, however, such a response is not so simple. While most countries’ militaries operate on a principle of “anything shy of a war crime is fair game,” Japan’s Self-Defense Forces operate in the opposite way and require very strict conditions before they can perform a certain action.

A good crash course in this can be found in our analysis on how the military can legally deal with a kaiju attack. Long story short, it is possible if Godzilla is classified as a “natural disaster” and the weapons used against him are classified as “tools” to neutralize the threat to Japan.

Zombies are much more complicated, however. Although certain aspects of the Godzilla scenario can be applied here, the fact that the threat is or was human introduces bigger legal hurdles for military and police forces. A video recently posted in the Legal Insight series by Tonari no Bengoshi Hosokyoku looks at this situation in-depth, but while their legal knowledge is spot-on, I’m concerned with some of their zombie awareness.

To start, much like with Godzilla, the SDF can be dispatched in a disaster relief capacity without issue. This means they can organize evacuations, set up barricades for shelters, and act in cases of self-defense to protect the public, just like police do. However, in this capacity, they cannot launch an assault on the zombies. One exception would be if the zombies were unleashed on Japan by a foreign government. This is the same reason that Godzilla cannot be considered an enemy combatant but King Ghidorah (sent by those jerks on Planet X) can.

So, let’s say our zombies are homegrown from some virus or mushrooms or something. Now, the question is whether they are people or not. According to Legal Insight, if they are classified as living people, then killing them can be considered murder, but even if they’re dead, filling them full of lead is also the crime of desecrating human remains.

However, Legal Insight also says that a zombie would be legally declared a corpse, and thus considered an “object” rather than a “person.” In this case, they could be treated in a way similar to wild animals that pose a threat to human life and be dealt with by the Self-Defense Forces using their  guns as “tools,” much like with Godzilla. The desecration of a corpse charges would be outweighed by the need to protect lives, much like how scuttling an abandoned ship adrift in the ocean is deemed necessary despite the destruction of property involved.

But I think that’s where they got it wrong.

Despite all of our advances, humans are still not great at determining if something is alive or not. For legal purposes, however, Japan employs the “three signs of death” (shi no sanchoko) used by medical professionals: cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, and loss of brainstem reflexes. If all three of these conditions are present at the same time and irreversible, then that person is deemed deceased.

Legal Insight says that zombies do exhibit the three signs of death, but I beg to differ. This is a problematic claim because there have been so many different zombie stories with zombies of wildly varying abilities, but even despite that, I don’t think any of them even exhibits one of the three signs of death, let alone all three.

Starting with cardiac arrest, zombies bleed when shot and clearly have muscle function, either of which would be impossible a beating heart. 

▼ Your Honor, if it pleases the court, I’d like to submit this gnarly video of Claire doming a couple zombies in Resident Evil 2 Remake. As you can clearly see from the blood spurting from their neckholes, they demonstrate arterial pressure which can only be achieved by a functioning heart.

And while they may not require it to function, zombies clearly breathe. How else do they make those “gnnnhhhurghhhh” noises? And brainstem reflexes? Baby, zombies are all about brainstem reflex.

▼ I’d now like to call Dr. Edwin Jenner of the CDC in the USA to the stand. He’ll explain to us that zombies have functioning brainstems beyond a shadow of a doubt.

So, whether it’s the ambling Night of the Living Dead zombies or your parkour-running 28 Days Later zombies, they are legally living humans and, as such, it could be argued that zombies would have rights in Japan. This means a cop or soldier cannot open fire on a zombie simply because they gave them a dirty look or even if they start walking towards them menacingly. The violence used against them must be in direct proportion to their own unlawful attack… which I guess means all soldiers can do is bite the zombies back.

So, in conclusion, the JSDF would be prohibited from gunning down zombies wholesale, and Japanese police would be legally obliged to arrest you for assault if one falls off the hood of your car while you drive away in a panic. That being said, in most zombie outbreaks the government seems to go down pretty quickly, and all laws just go out the window anyway.

Happy Halloween!

title: Guile cosplay goes with everyone for Halloween at SoraNews24 HQ [Photos]
description: Go home and be a family man? Nah, we have to go to work. We keep SoraNews24 HQ clean enough so that we don’t have flies on the wall, but if you were to be, for instance, a shapeshifting tanuki disguised as a fern in the corner of our office on Friday, you might have […]
content:
Go home and be a family man? Nah, we have to go to work.

We keep SoraNews24 HQ clean enough so that we don’t have flies on the wall, but if you were to be, for instance, a shapeshifting tanuki disguised as a fern in the corner of our office on Friday, you might have heard the following conversation take place.

Mr. Sato: “Hey, you guys bring your Guile gear?”

P.K.: “Yeah.”

Mr. Sato: “OK. So, we doing this?”

Ahiruneko: “We sure are. But, like, I really didn’t have much to bring.”

Mr. Sato: “But, like, -how- are we supposed to do this? We just, like, become Guile?”

Seiji Nakazawa: “Sure. No need to overthink it, right?”

P.K.: “We all just turn into Guile, just like that?”

See, we have a tradition here at SoraNews24, where everyone who’s in the office on the day closest to Halloween dresses up in costume. We try to have some sort of theme, like dressing up as the trendiest desert drink of the year or trying to transform into actual parts of the Tokyo cityscape. This year, we settled on the theme of developer Capcom’s hit fighting video game series, Street Fighter, and since every release since Street Fighter II: Championship Edition has allowed players to pick the same character as each other, we decided that everyone in the office would become Guile.

Mr. Sato: “I think everybody already has their outfit sorted, so we better get started on our making our Guile hair.”

Takeshi Harada: “How are we supposed to do that?”

Mr. Sato: “All you need is some yellow paper, and some imagination.”

With Hollywood’s newest live-action Street Fighter adaptation currently playing in theaters, some might be tempted to accuse us of trying to piggyback on the movie’s hype train, but our Guile-loving credentials have been an established matter of public record for some time, as we previously published a literally hard-hitting investigative piece on the real-world effectiveness of Guile’s iconically cool-looking low-guard pose from the games.

Takeshi: “Am I doing it right?”

Mr. Sato: “Hey, man, you gotta trust your own judgement when making Guile hair.”

Then, after 20 minutes of cutting, taping, and changing clothes in a wide-open office with no locker room…

Mr. Sato: “OK, everybody set? Show us your Guiles!”

So, uh, as you can see, even though everyone was dressed as the same character, there was still plenty of, let’s call them individual creative differences present in the final results.

Let’s take a closer look at what everyone came up with.

▼ Seiji Guile!

▼ Yuichiro Guile!

▼ Ahiruneko Guile!

▼ Takeshi Guile!

▼ P.K. Guile!

▼ Yoshio Guile!

▼ Sato Guile!

▼ Go Hatori Guile, who actually wasn’t in the office this day but who joined the battle via a photo taken ahead of time!

So who’s Guile was the best Guile? We left that judgement up to Seiji, since we felt like we kind of owed him one for all the physical punishment he took in that Guile blocking test.

Seiji Guile: “All right, you maggots! Line up for inspection!”

Seiji Guile: “Sato Guile! You are the sorriest display of a Guile in this whole company!”

Sato Guile: “What? But I thought I did pretty good. I even worked out extra to tone up my arms and shoulders for this.”

Seiji Guile: “I didn’t expect anything more of you than using paper for your hair, but why did you put the crease in the front? That’s inexcusable! You’re a disgrace to our proud Guile traditions!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! Yoshio Guile! You’re all right. I can tell you’re taking the mission seriously.”

Seiji Guile: “Unlike the rest of these knuckleheads who just used drawing paper, you reinforced your spikes with construction paper. That’s the kind of ingenuity that we need to be ready to display in the field.”

Yoshio Guile: “Sir! Thank you, sir!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! Ahiruneko Guile! What in the name of a redizzy combo do you call this?”

Ahiruneko Guile: “No good?”

Seiji Guile: “No good at all! That sloppy, loose tank top is totally outside uniform regulations!”

Ahiruneko Guile: “Well, I mean, I just bought it on Amazon, so it wasn’t like I could try it on and check the fit or anything…”

Seiji Guile: “You think Guile would be caught dead in something like that? You’re a disgrace to the uniform!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! P.K. Guile!”

P.K. Guile: “Look, I’ll just get it out of the way and apologize right now.”

Seiji Guile: “Well, at least you’ve got a scrap of self awareness. You know your pants are wrong, right?”

P.K. Guile: “When I went to the thrift shop, this was all they had for camo pants. I know the color is wrong.”

Seiji Guile: “No, actually Guile has alternate color versions with blue pants, so that’s not the problem. But what no one has ever seen is Guile rolling up his pants!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! Takeshi Guile!”

Seiji Guile: “You clearly didn’t understand the assignment either! A digital camouflage pattern? Seriously? You know Guile doesn’t wear that!”

Takeshi Guile: “I went to a thrift store too, and this was the only pair of camo pants I could find.”

Seiji Guile: “You’re endangering the whole mission by relying on thrift stores! Next time shop online if you need to and make sure you get the pattern right!”

Seiji Guile: “Next! Yuichiro Guile! Let’s wrap this up!”

Seiji Guile: “So tell me how you managed to forget you’re supposed to be Guile? You look like you just came from the kitchen or the beach!”

Seiji Guile: “That hairline’s crammed all the way down onto your eyebrows, like you’re wearing chef’s hat! And shorts? Shorts?!! How’re you gonna have a proper street fight without proper pants?”

Seiji Guile: “Aside from Yoshio and Go, none of you are ready to be Guile! Guess it’s up to me to whip you all into shape.”

Guiles: “Yes, sir!”

Seiji Guile: “ATTEN-TION! Company, form up and…flash kick charge pose!”

Guiles: “Yes, sir!”

Seiji Guile: “Crouching guard!”

Guiles: “Yes, sir!”

Seiji Guile: “Just you wait and see! I’ll turn you all into real Guiles yet!”

A Happy Halloween to all of you reading SoraNews24! Whether you’re out trick-or-treating or partying with friends, we hope you have a safe and fun October 31, and that no one cheeses you with invisible throws.

title: Cold Stone is closing its final branch in all of east Japan, but it’s going down singing
description: Parting is such very, very sweet sorrow. No one’s really watching their calories on October 31, right? Between trick-or-treating, Halloween parties, and all those tempting candy displays in the stores, there’s no better occasion for indulging your sweet tooth multiple times during the same day. And if you’re already leaving room for desserts, this Halloween […]
content:
Parting is such very, very sweet sorrow.

No one’s really watching their calories on October 31, right? Between trick-or-treating, Halloween parties, and all those tempting candy displays in the stores, there’s no better occasion for indulging your sweet tooth multiple times during the same day. And if you’re already leaving room for desserts, this Halloween is a very good time to make a visit to Cold Stone, because on October 31 they’re permanently closing their last remaining branch in east Japan.

Cold Stone’s time in Japan has been a rollercoaster ride. The chain first showed up in Japan in 2005 and became an immediate sensation among sweets fans, with long lines forming to try the offerings of the American “creamery” and listening to the staff’s cheerful singing voices while they waited. For a while there, Cold Stone looked poised to enter the ranks of Japan’s lovingly adopted brands from the U.S. such as McDonald’s and Starbuck’s. Unfortunately, not long after Cold Stone Japan’s expansion plans heated up, consumer enthusiasm for the chain started to cool off. In time, branches started closing down, with the even vacating Tokyo entirely for a while.

Eventually, though, Cold Stone found its way back to the capital. In 2023, it opened a new branch Tokyo’s Tama district, and then another in downtown’s trendy Harajuku neighborhood.

▼ The Harajuku branch, shortly after its opening in June of 2023

Sadly, neither of those comeback bids panned out, and by April of 2025, there were once again no Cold Stone branches anywhere in Tokyo, and the only remaining location in all of east Japan was located inside an outlet shopping mall in Tochigi Prefecture…which closed down one month later.

But then this past summer came a ray of hope for Cold Stone fans in east Japan with the opening of a Cold Stone branch in the town of Kamakura in Kanagawa Prefecture, Tokyo’s neighbor to the south. Kamakura is a major sightseeing destination, with temples, shrines, hiking trails, and beaches, and it’s only about an hour by train from Tokyo, making it an easy daytrip for Tokyoites and travelers staying at hotels in the capital.

▼ Video of the Kamakura Cold Stone’s opening day on July 30

View this post on Instagram

Being a big Cold Stone fan, our ace reporter Mr. Sato was thrilled to have the chain back in east Japan, and was looking forward to getting a scoop or two the next time he was down in Kamakura. The urgency on his plans to visit the city got rapidly cranked up, though, when on October 29 Cold Stone Japan announced through its official Instagram account that it would be permanently closing its Kamakura branch, and doing so in just two days’ time, on October 31.

So Mr. Sato dropped everything, dashed to the station, and rode the train to Kamakura.

The Kamakura Cold Stone has a pretty good location. It’s outside JR Kamakura Station’s west exit, which isn’t as busy and developed as the east side of the structure, but there’s still a decent amount of foot traffic, especially since the shop is close to the transfer gates for the Enoden rail line that runs along the shore and provides ironically picturesque views.

At this point, Mr. Sato might still have been able to delude himself into believing that there’d been some kind of mistake in Cold Stone’s Instagram announcement, and that the store wasn’t actually shutting down after just three months in business. But sure enough, there was a written notice posted at the counter that said:

Cold Stone Creamery Kamakura Station
Notice of closure

We are grateful to the support shown by so many visitors since our opening. As of October 31, Cold Stone Creamery Kamakura Station will be closing.

We wish to take this opportunity to sincerely thank all of our customers. We will continue to do our best to provide all of you with Happy Creamery experiences.

We look forward to seeing all of your smiles again someday. Thank you so much for everything.

So this was really going to be goodbye. Carefully weighing his options for this final Cold Stone session, Mr. Sato asked for Dobai chocolate ice cream in a chocolate waffle bowl, covered with chocolate sauce. “Is it OK if we sing?” asked the staff, unwaveringly cheerful, even now, and Mr. Sato said “Yes! Please!”

“I was sad to hear you’ll be closing.” Said Mr. Sato after the song was finished and they handed him his order. “Yes, we only found out about it two days ago,” said the clerk, revealing that they’d apparently been as surprised as Mr. Sato was at the turn of events.

▼ Mr. Sato’s ice cream. He does not fool around when it comes to grand finales of his favorite dessert places.

Mr. Sato couldn’t help silently wondering why it had to end like this. It’s not like Japan doesn’t like ice cream. As a matter of fact, Japan loves ice cream. Baskin-Robbins has over 1,000 branches in Japan, including one on the other side of Kamakura Station. Aside from specialty shops, fast food chains and snack stands sell ice cream all year round, as do convenience stores and super markets.

So why can’t Cold Stone seem to get a stronger foothold in the country? The company hasn’t made any official statement explaining its woes, but as we’ve discussed before, it might have something to do with the kind of ice cream that Cold Stone serves not matching up with how Japan would like it served. Ice cream fans in Japan are fine with casual settings or eating on the go for simple frozen treats, like a modest-sized scoop of Baskin-Robbins or personal-size serving of Häagen-Dazs. On the other end of the spectrum, leisurely savoring a large, decadent parfait at a cozy or fashionable cafe is considered a highlight-of-the-day-caliber experience. Cold Stone, though, doesn’t really fit into either of those two scenarios. Their desserts are big, heavy, and potentially messy, the sort of thing that Japanese sweets fans usually want to sit down and take their time with, but Cold Stone’s focus has always been primarily on take-out, and that incongruent combination is likely a limiting factor in terms of the chain’s potential appeal to a broad demographic in Japan.

This does, though, leave the limited demographic of passionate Cold Stone fans like Mr. Sato in an unfortunate position, though, since even if they do exist, there apparently just aren’t enough of them to keep Cold Stone a viable venture. It’s enough to bring a tear to your eye…but after hearing the staff bravely sing as they put together his order, Mr. Sato knew that if he was going to have to say goodbye, again, he was going to say goodbye with a smile.

The October 31 closing means that, as of November 1, there will be only one remaining Cold Stone in all of Japan, located in the Mitsui Outlet Park Jazz Dream Nagashima in Mie Prefecture. Even taking the Shinkansen, it takes about three hours to get there from Tokyo, so Mr. Sato’s first wish would be for Cold Stone to rest up and make one more comeback attempt in the Tokyo area, but if they can’t, he might just need to book some bullet train tickets the next time his cravings hit.

Open 10 a.m.-6 p.m.

title: Life-size Monster Hunter dragon statues to be built at Japanese shopping mall
description: Here there be dragons and bargains. Generally, people don’t go to malls to buy daily necessities like paper towels or detergent. Mall shopping is primarily for fun or special-occasion purposes, and to make the atmosphere even more fun and special, sometimes outlet malls in Japan have collaborations with popular video game franchises. Maybe they put […]
content:
Here there be dragons and bargains.

Generally, people don’t go to malls to buy daily necessities like paper towels or detergent. Mall shopping is primarily for fun or special-occasion purposes, and to make the atmosphere even more fun and special, sometimes outlet malls in Japan have collaborations with popular video game franchises. Maybe they put up a Final Fantasy Christmas tree for the holiday season, or set out some Super Mario cardboard character standees.

And then there’s what Mitsui Outlet Park Fukuoka Marinoa is planning to do for its team-up with the Monster Hunter franchise.

Two different giant beasts from developer Capcom’s hit series are scheduled to becoming residents of the mall, and we do mean giant beasts, as these statues will be “life-size” versions of Fire Wyvern Rathalos, known as the King of the Skies, and Leviathan Lagiacrus, King of the Seas.

Because Monster Hunter’s gameplay system allows for variances in individual specimen sizes, we can’t say for sur how large the statues of Rathalos and Lagiacrus will be, but the preview images promise that they’ll be of sufficient stature that low-level adventurers would be ill-advised to attempt to solo them.

Since the Monster Hunter: World installment in the series, particularly bold monsters have been able to engage in turf wars with one another should they both covet the same section of the environment, and it looks like Mitsui Outlet Park Fukuoka Marinoa’s Rathalos and Lagiacrus might not be the best of friends, as effects such as dramatic sound, lighting, and mist will be used to simulate battles between the two.

The outlet mall, located near Meinohama Station in Fukuoka City, is slated to open this coming April, so you’ve got a few months to sort out your travel plans/put together a Monster Hunter team before the creatures appear.

title: Evangelion announces collaboration with Hard Rock Cafe
description: Get in the Hard Rock crossover, Shinji! The Hard Rock Cafe currently has two branches in Tokyo, one in the Roppongi Neighborhood and one attached to Ueno Station, but what if the restaurant had a Tokyo-3 branch? And no, we don’t mean a third branch in Tokyo, but a branch inside Tokyo-3, the city that serves […]
content:
Get in the Hard Rock crossover, Shinji!

The Hard Rock Cafe currently has two branches in Tokyo, one in the Roppongi Neighborhood and one attached to Ueno Station, but what if the restaurant had a Tokyo-3 branch? And no, we don’t mean a third branch in Tokyo, but a branch inside Tokyo-3, the city that serves as the main setting of Evangelion.

That’s the concept behind a new collaboration between the giant robot anime series and music-themed restaurant chain, which has led to a new collection of crossover merch. Evangelion Unit-01 is the star here, featured on T-shirts with its iconic green-and-purple color scheme and AT field hexagonal pattern applied to the Hard Rock Logo.

Three different colors are on offer, with white available at the Roppongi, Ueno Kyoto, and Universal Citywalk Osaka Hard Rock Cafes. Gray shirts will be on the rack at Roppongi, Yokohama, Citywalk Osaka, and the Namba store, while those looking for black shirts will find them at Ueno, Yokohama, Kyoto, and Namba.

Also part of the lineup is a sukajan/Yokosuka jacket, which seems like a very appropriate canvas for this sort of East-meets-West endeavor.

Rounding out the fashion selection is the Eva/Hard Rock cap, and Unit-01 and the series’ core pilot roster will also be appearing on shot glasses, magnets, and pins.

The magnet and shot glass, pictures above, will include the name of the city in which they were purchased, but the pins will be specific to each Hard Rock location.

The pins are limited-quantity items, with only 500 of each design being made and carrying a price of 3,080 yen (US$19), which is also the price of the magnet. The shot glass, meanwhile, is 1,980 yen, the shirts 5,940 yen, and the Yokosuka jacket, as is often the case for the embroidered garments, is a premium piece, at 66,000 yen. While supplies last, fans purchasing the collaboration items will get them placed inside an Evangelion/Hard Rock shopping bag.

The lineup goes on sale November 3, with the exception of the pin which is scheduled to be available sometime in “early November.”

title: Burger King Japan shuns Shibuya Halloween spirit, but keeps it alive everywhere else
description: No tricks or treats is the plan at Shibuya Center-gai, but cool sweets will be waiting at every other branch. In a way, I suppose you could accuse Burger King Japan of having lost its Halloween spirit. The chain’s Shibuya Center-gai branch in downtown Tokyo, just a short walk from the world-famous Shibuya Scramble intersection, […]
content:
No tricks or treats is the plan at Shibuya Center-gai, but cool sweets will be waiting at every other branch.

In a way, I suppose you could accuse Burger King Japan of having lost its Halloween spirit. The chain’s Shibuya Center-gai branch in downtown Tokyo, just a short walk from the world-famous Shibuya Scramble intersection, announced on Thursday that it’ll be closed for the entirety of October 31. The storefront’s shutter will be down with a large 臨時休業 (“temporarily closed”) written across it, and the Burger King logo will even have an X over it to quickly communicate the message “No burgers here on Halloween!”

This has become something of an annual tradition at the Shibuya Center-gai Burger King, stemming from the neighborhood’s attempts to clean up its image at Halloween. Shibuya was one of the first places in Japan where people began gathering in large numbers to celebrate Halloween, and what started as good-natured fun eventually turned into alcohol-soaked street parties with instances of vandalism, theft, and violence marring the unsanctioned gatherings.

In recent years the authorities have been cracking down with measures such as restricting alcohol sales and setting up gates and barricades to more tightly control the flow of people in and out of Shibuya on and around Halloween night, as well as public awareness campaigns reminding people that public drinking, littering, and other forms of inconsiderate or unruly behavior are not allowed. And while there’s no government mandate prohibiting Burger King from staying open on October 31, the restaurant’s management evidently feels the wisest choice is to close the place and take the day off so as not to contribute to overcrowding in Shibuya on Halloween.

That doesn’t mean that Burger King Japan is opposed to Halloween fun in general, though. As a matter of fact, at the same time that the Shibuya Center-gai location is closed, every other Burger King in Japan will be actively celebrating by inviting people to come on in and trick-or-treat!

On October 31, all non-Shibuya Center-gai Burger Kings will be giving out free soft serve ice cream to the first 30 visitors age 18 or younger who come up to the counter and say “trick or treat.” There doesn’t appear to be any requirement that they order anything else, either, so this really is following the classic Halloween custom of giving out sweets simply for the asking. They’re even sweetening the free-sweets deal by tossing in a sheet of Halloween stickers.

▼ The ice cream here appears to be haunted, but that’s still better than not having ice cream right?

Note, though, that the trick-or-treat ice cream is only available between 2 p.m. and 6 p.m., which means no having it for breakfast, but since trick-or-treating isn’t a morning activity, even this is in keeping with the spirit of Halloween.

title: Hello Kitty cuts ties with hit Japanese spy drama Vivant over torture scenes
description: Goodbye Kitty. Vivant has emerged as a major hit on Japanese TV to a degree that only seems to come along every decade or so. It stars Masato Sakai, who also starred in Japan’s last gigantic TV hit Hanzawa Naoki, by the same director, with Sakai this time playing a businessman who gets embroiled in […]
content:
Goodbye Kitty.

Vivant has emerged as a major hit on Japanese TV to a degree that only seems to come along every decade or so. It stars Masato Sakai, who also starred in Japan’s last gigantic TV hit Hanzawa Naoki, by the same director, with Sakai this time playing a businessman who gets embroiled in international intrigue.

The program has become so popular that it is frequently involved in tie-ups with other brands eager to ride the Vivant wave. And there is perhaps no company that loves collaborating more than Sanrio, which has teamed up with just about everything from Sesame Street and Clinique to Pringles and Godzilla.

Earlier this year, various goods such as plush toys and T-shirts featured six of Sanrio’s most popular characters dressed as the characters from Vivant. Nogitty was a mash-up of Hello Kitty and Sakai’s character Yusuke Nogi, while Hangyodon took on the role of Mamoru Nozaki, played by Hiroshi Abe in the show. There were also My Melody, Pompompurin, Cinnamoroll, and Kuromi as Kaoru Yuzuki, Drum, Nokoru, and Kurosu respectively.

＼明日まで／

G階段下ワゴンで開催中の
VIVANT POP-UP SHOPは7/16の18時まで！

グッズをゲットして、
7/26(日)から始まるTBS系日曜劇場『#VIVANT』第2シーズンを観よう！#サンリオキャラクターズ#東京キャラクターストリート#キャラスト pic.twitter.com/lOJhVVmhI7

— 【公式】東京キャラクターストリート (@characterstreet) July 15, 2026

I’m using past tense there because as of 29 October, all of the Sanrio Vivant items have been taken off the market. On October 28, Sanrio’s Chinese arm, Sanrio Shanghai International Trading, announced, through its social media account, the cancellation of Sanrio’s collaboration with Vivant and that all future activities related to it would be cancelled as well. Sanrio Japan also posted a statement on October 29 announcing the cancelation of the collaboration, apologizing for any discomfort it may have caused and that the themes of the show were inconsistent with Sanrio’s corporate philosophy of “One world, connecting smiles.”

A few days earlier, Chinese state-run media had published a piece on Vivant, accusing it of slandering China and “exaggerating the China threat theory,” referring to the idea that China’s rapid growth poses a fundamental threat to global peace and stability. This all stems from scenes in Vivant that show a fictional organization affiliated with China brutally torturing members of the fictional Japanese covert group Beppan, hacking all of the fingers off one member’s hand.

Problematic Japanese-Chinese relations aside, reading that last sentence would make one wonder what Hello Kitty was doing with this show in the first place. Granted, Sanrio has been known to dabble in dark franchises in the past, but close association with torture and mutilation might not be good optics for the maker of Dokidoki Yummychums. It’s an opinion shared by many in online comments as well.

“It was an odd combination to begin with.”
“I always thought Sanrio avoided collaborating with themes involving things like the military or war. How did Vivant get the green light?”
“I guess this was a miscalculation on Sanrio’s part. Maybe they didn’t anticipate this kind of explicit and controversial content from Vivant.”
“It was cancelled before I could buy anything! I was planning to get something next month, too.”
“This is hardly surprising. I’m guessing Masato Sakai won’t be finding much work in China either.”
“Sanrio needs to put more thought into who they team up with.“

As for Vivant’s response to the criticism from China, the network that airs it, TBS, released a statement saying they will seriously consider questions that the show “harbors hostility towards certain countries” and features excessive violence. While they maintain that the torture scenes were necessary to the show’s story, they also say they will continue to carefully consider whether certain depictions will cause discomfort or excessive fear among viewers.

We’ll see how that goes, but hopefully Hello Kitty learned her lesson and will stick with more family-friendly fare like It… I’m guessing they didn’t read the book.

Source: Sponichi Annex, Hachima Kiko, Sanrio

title: Real-world Legend of Zelda treasures, Heart Container lights and Ruppe pouches, coming soon [Pics]
description: Whether you’re restoring your energy at home or out adventuring in the world, these Hyrulian artifacts will be ready to help. Nintendo fans already have November 5 circled on their calendars, since that’s when the long-awaited remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time goes on sale for the Switch 2. That’s not the […]
content:
Whether you’re restoring your energy at home or out adventuring in the world, these Hyrulian artifacts will be ready to help.

Nintendo fans already have November 5 circled on their calendars, since that’s when the long-awaited remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time goes on sale for the Switch 2. That’s not the only cool Zelda-related release coming up in November though, with Japanese fashion and interior company Takarajimasha, whose name means “treasure island company,” releasing two creations based on treasure from Nintendo’s fantasy franchise.

The first item is a replica of the coveted Heart Container, which has been extending the hero Link’s maximum life bar since the very start of the series. Takarajimasha’s version is modeled on the version seen in Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom with its arabesque gold framing.

While this real-world won’t instantly increase your longevity or resilience, it can provide illumination, as it’s actually a 9-centimeter (3.5-inch) tall lamp that produces a warm red glow when switched on.

The designers know that you will want to hold this in your hands, so the lamp can be detached from the base.

▼ Though you’ll have to hum Zelda’s traditional four-note “treasure found” fanfare yourself.

Because of their value and rarity, Heart Containers are something that players search high and low for in exploring the games’ realms, but Takarajimasha also wants to salute the most common of Zelda treasures, the humble Rupee.

The green Ruppe, the smallest-denomination of Hyrulian currency, is something you’ll collect hundreds of, if not thousands, during a playthrough of one of the Zelda games, and yet, it’s still sure to bring a smile to you, or any fellow fans, when one shows up in our world as a zippered silicone pouch.

The designers bill is as a komono ire, a Japanese term whose closest English equivalent would be “accessory pouch,” but really refers to a pouch for storing any small items, such as earbuds, cosmetics, or even bite-sized snacks.

There’s a strap in case you want to use it as a bag charm, and you’ll also find The Legend of Zelda, written in Japanese, on the Rupee’s underside.

A quirk of the Japanese publishing industry is that fashion and lifestyle magazines sometimes come with some sort of fashion/lifestyle item bundled with them. Sometimes these are so popular that they overshadow the edition of the periodical, so, noticing this, companies like Takarajimasha that specialize in such bundled items sometimes flip the script and make the items the primary product and toss in a mini magazine as a supplementary freebie. Both the Heart Container Interior Light and the Rupee Silicone Pouch are being offered in this format, branded as “Books” and sold together with an eight-page booklet of undisclosed but presumably Zelda-related nature.

The Heart Container light is priced at 3,839 yen (US$24) and the Rupee pouch at 2,992 yen. They both go on sale November 2 and can be ordered, here and here, through the Takarajimasha online shop as well as through select branches of convenience store chain Lawson.

title: Modern exosuits are opening up ancient Japanese castle climbs to everyone
description: Combining palanquins and muscle suits to make historic sites accessible for all. Along the eastern shores of Lake Biwa, Japan’s largest freshwater lake, in Shiga is the city of Hikone, home to one of only twelve castles in Japan with its original main keep still standing. However, reaching the top is not a casual stroll, […]
content:
Combining palanquins and muscle suits to make historic sites accessible for all.

Along the eastern shores of Lake Biwa, Japan’s largest freshwater lake, in Shiga is the city of Hikone, home to one of only twelve castles in Japan with its original main keep still standing.

However, reaching the top is not a casual stroll, being guarded by 140 steep, irregular stone steps explicitly designed to exhaust invading samurai, and now those same steps present a modern dilemma.

Being a National Special Historic Site, and a possible candidate for UNESCO World Cultural Heritage status in 2028, how can the site be made more accessible for visitors who use wheelchairs or have mobility impairments, especially when pouring concrete ramps over 17th-century masonry isn’t exactly an option that would be enthusiastically received?

On October 19, Hikone City staff and volunteers conducted a trial, where they took turns acting as carriers, carrying wheelchair users up to the main enclosure (honmaru) using a traditional wooden mountain palanquin (yamakago). The trek covered a 285-meter (935-foot) round-trip with a 50-meter (165-foot) vertical rise and an average 18-percent incline, which is not an easy feat for two people to do.

So, to lighten the load for the team of six carriers, trial participants strapped on state-of-the-art, non-motorized wearable assist suits, with two wearing the Muscle Suit Soft-Power Easy-Lift and four equipping the Mediaid Firm Guard Waist EX Hard.

▼Muscle Suit Soft-Power Easy-Lift

▼Mediaid Firm Guard Waist EX Hard

The reaction from the carriers was enthusiastic, receiving comments like:
“Because I injured my lower back in the past, wearing it gave me a real sense of security.”
“It is attached at the base of the knees, but when standing upright it is loose, so it does not get in the way of going up and down the stairs.”
“The moment I took it off, I realized just how much it had been helping me.”

Standing up while balancing a palanquin on your shoulders normally feels like tipping backward, causing some difficulty in maintaining balance, but the back-and-leg support makes rising smooth and stable.

Beyond opening up easier physical access to a historic tourist site, the trial offered a glimpse into an exciting future for Japanese tourism, with accompanying curators explaining the history and scenery of the location, creating an opportunity for visitors to get a taste of what it would be like to travel around the mountain like nobility in the time of the samurai.

Similarly, it could also open up another bucket-list item for many travelers along with sitting on the back of a human-powered rickshaw, being chauffeured around Japan’s historical districts. If wearable assist suits can help bridge the gap between 17th-century architecture and 21st-century accessibility, it opens up countless possibilities for historic castles, mountain temples, and heritage sites all across Japan.

title: Studio Ghibli homeware brand’s faux oil lamp brings light, smiles, and Kiki’s Jiji to your home
description: Kiki’s Delivery Service scene-stealer is adorably transfixed by Donguri Kyowakoku’s latest homeware offering. Any branch of Ghibli specialty shop chain Donguri Kyowakoku will be filled with amazing merch from the anime studio’s films, but a few locations are extra-special thanks to their inclusion of items from the Donguri Closet sub-brand. As the name alludes to, […]
content:
Kiki’s Delivery Service scene-stealer is adorably transfixed by Donguri Kyowakoku’s latest homeware offering.

Any branch of Ghibli specialty shop chain Donguri Kyowakoku will be filled with amazing merch from the anime studio’s films, but a few locations are extra-special thanks to their inclusion of items from the Donguri Closet sub-brand. As the name alludes to, Donguri Closet’s focus is on fashion and home décor. The designs have an elegant coziness to them, making them the sort of things that, without being flashy, will catch the eyes of fans as soon as they step into the room…and, in this case, catch the eyes of Kiki’s Delivery Service’s Jiji too.

So what’s got Kiki’s black cat companion so captivated? A recreation of an oil lamp seen in the home of Osono, the kindly baker who Kiki and Jiji rent a room from after arriving in the city where the anime’s story takes place. Though made of resin and ABS for extra sturdiness, the intricate details and delicate coloring give it a look evocative of antique porcelain.

The clear top section of the lamp is made of glass, but since the logistics hassles and safety risks of burning an actual oil lamp can be a hassle to deal with, this is an electric light. The designers have cleverly hid the main power switch on the underside of the base, though, to better sell the illusion of old-timey-ness, and the light can be turned on or off with a tap of your finger thanks to a touch sensor embedded in the lamp.

Officially called the Kiki’s Delivery Service Mini Lamp-Mitsumeru Jiji (“Transfixed Jiji”), the piece is 12.8 centimeters (5 inches) tall and 11.2 centimeters wide, putting it right in that sweet spot where it’s neither too small to be noticed nor too big to be in the way. Priced at 13,200 yen (US$83), it’ll be available at select Donguri Kyowakoku stores in Tokyo (Ikebukuro, Skytree Town Solamachi), Nagoya (Takashimaya Gate Tower Mall), Osaka (Lucua Osaka), Fukuoka (Canal City Hakata), and Sapporo (Sapporo Parco), as well as through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here starting October 31.

title: Japanese government still lists refusing to pay for dates as a form of domestic violence
description: Once again, there’s a lot of nuance that’s lost in the attempt to be succinct. As you can probably guess from its name, the Japanese government’s Gender Equality Bureau isn’t a fan of imbalance in interpersonal relationships. What is surprising to many people, though, is the bureau’s assertion that “not paying for any dating expenses” […]
content:
Once again, there’s a lot of nuance that’s lost in the attempt to be succinct.

As you can probably guess from its name, the Japanese government’s Gender Equality Bureau isn’t a fan of imbalance in interpersonal relationships. What is surprising to many people, though, is the bureau’s assertion that “not paying for any dating expenses” is committing an act of domestic violence.

On its website, the bureau lists four categories of “dating domestic violence.” Examples of “physical violence” are pretty obvious – striking, pulling hair, throwing objects, that sort of thing. “Sexual violence,” the bureau says, includes coerced sex, refusal to use contraception, and nonconsensual naked photography or video recording. “Psychological violence” is described as making insulting or disrespectful remarks, forbidding a romantic partner from seeing their friends, or monitoring their email communications.

It’s bureau discussion of “economic violence,” though, that’s been raising some eyebrows online in Japan this week. While one could argue that this is using the word “violence” in its broadest possible sense, most of the examples are things that would be considered wrong under basic common sense/decency, such as not paying back money borrowed from a romantic partner, taking money from their bank account without permission, and forbidding them to work outside the home or forcing them to quit their job. But then there’s this example of economic violence:

“Not paying for any dating expenses.”

Japan may not have a reputation for being the most chivalrous society, and going Dutch, or warikan, as it’s called in Japanese, is more common in casual dating here than it is in some other countries. That said, it’s not at all unusual for guys to pay for everything on a date with a girl, and the government of Japan saying that this is a form of domestic violence has been provoking a lot of responses online to a recent Twitter post pointing out the bureau’s stance.

“Yeah, it’s practically theft, so it’s obviously a form of domestic abuse.”
“Wait, I’ve never made a girl pay on a date, so does that mean that I’ve been subjected to economic violence in the eyes of the government?”
“There are a lot of guys who are the victim of this kind of domestic abuse.”
“Does this make guys who habitually treat the girl on dates masochists for actively encouraging dating domestic violence?”
“Let’s all make sure to properly split the bill, because the government has said that anything other than that is considered economic violence, OK?”
“That’ll show all those gold-digger girls who hang out in Tokyo’s Minato Ward.”
“This is wonderful for men. I think all us guys are thinking ‘Hey, can’t you pitch in a little?’ but we can’t say it to the girl because we’re trying to look cool.”
“Coerced treating is a crime.”
“I think they mean it’s wrong for both guys and girls to refuse to pay for dating expenses.”

There’s probably at least a little wry humor behind some of those comments, but the last two are the ones that really get to the heart of the matter. As clarified by a spokesperson for the Gender Equality Bureau when this example of economic violence also became a topic of online discussion a few years ago, the bureau recognizes that “Both men and women can be victims of this kind of violence” and that “If both sides are OK with [one person not paying], it’s not domestic violence.” It’s when one person attempts to force their partner to shoulder all of the dating costs against their will that it crosses the line into unacceptable behavior, or when someone demands to be reimbursed for past dating expenses that, at the time, they offered to pay for.

▼ Just like going to a butcher shop on a date is fine if that’s what both you and your sweetheart are into, so too is it OK if you’re in agreement that you’ll be treating her to a half-kilo of ground beef.

In other words, the bureau’s guidelines are more about discouraging someone from unilaterally declaring “We’re going out, and you’re going to pay for me” or becoming verbally abusive if asked to chip in, not shaming someone for consistently accepting offers to be treated. But while we’re on the subject of “other words,” as mentioned above, this is not the first time the vague language used on the bureau’s website regarding who pays on a date has caused confusion, and the list of examples being followed by the declaration that “All of these are violence” leaves the door open to misinterpretation that context and a couple’s specific circumstances are irrelevant. The statement has remained on the site in its current form since 2018, so maybe it’s time for an update that puts a finer point on things.

Source: Gender Equality Bureau, Hachima Kiko, Twitter/@anzuchanw

title: Starbucks Japan releases “Let’s Par-TEA!” Frappuccino and drinks for the holiday season
description: Each beverage has its own unique character so you can choose which one you’d like to party with. With the holiday season fast approaching, Starbucks is bringing the party spirit to its stores in Japan with a trio of new drinks based around the theme of “Let’s par-TEA!” As the name suggests, the three new holiday […]
content:
Each beverage has its own unique character so you can choose which one you’d like to party with.

With the holiday season fast approaching, Starbucks is bringing the party spirit to its stores in Japan with a trio of new drinks based around the theme of “Let’s par-TEA!” As the name suggests, the three new holiday drinks shine a spotlight on tea, with strawberry, royal milk tea and Earl Grey chocolate featuring in the beverages.

The three stars of this tea party each have their own distinct character, so you can choose the one that best suits your mood. Those wanting an elegant pick-me-up can opt for the Joyful Medley Strawberry Creamy Tea Latte, which combines robust black tea with the smooth sweetness of oolong tea and the floral fragrance of jasmine tea, finished with a subtle hint of apricot.

▼ Joyful Medley Strawberry Creamy Tea Latte (Tall size only, 638 yen [US$4.03] for takeout; 650 yen for dine-in)

The blended tea base is joined by sweetened fresh cream and a topping of strawberry-flavoured mousse and freeze-dried strawberries. The rich aroma of the chain’s famous Joyful Medley blend, which is reminiscent of apricot jam, is layered with creamy sweetness, while the finish remains refreshing, allowing you to enjoy a variety of tastes and aromas throughout the beverage.

▼ Earl Grey Chocolate Frappuccino (Tall size only, 678 yen takeout; 690 yen dine-in)

Those wanting a little more playfulness can reward themselves with this tea-and-chocolate Frappuccino, which combines aromatic Earl Grey with rich chocolate sauce and crunchy chocolate chips. It has a mellow, layered flavour, with the gentle fragrance of bergamot and the taste of black tea spreading through the palate with every sip, while the chocolate chips add crunchy textural contrast, capturing the playful spirit of the holiday season.

▼ Royal Milk Tea (609 yen takeout; 620 yen dine-in)

Finally, we have a rich, blended milk tea that combines milk with an original blend of three teas: Darjeeling, Assam and Ceylon. The full-bodied flavour of the tea harmonises with the mellow creaminess of the milk, creating a rich and rewarding taste that tea lovers will fall in love with.

As an extra special holiday treat, Starbucks is also adding a cookie option, so you can add more flavour and a dash of cuteness to any iced beverage that’s topped with whipped cream or mousse foam.

▼ Be a Santa Cookie Topping (69 yen takeout; 70 yen dine-in)

The “Be a Santa Cookie Topping” has a buttery aroma and crisp yet crumbly shortbread texture. The three designs – a present, a Christmas tree and a Santa hat – are provided at random so, like a Christmas present, you won’t know what you’re getting until it’s given to you by the barista.

While the cookie topping will be available while stocks last from 2-19 November, the drinks will be on the menu for a limited (but unspecified) time from 2 November.

title: Shinkansen online ticketing service reports customer data leak
description: Online reservation system handles tickets for Shinkansen’s “Golden Route” and Kyushu. If you’re planning to take a ride on the Shinkansen, the Smart EX online ticketing service is a handy utility. Managed by Shinkansen operator Central Japan Railway Company/JR Central, Smart EX lets you book seats on bullet trains running in eastern and western Japan, […]
content:
Online reservation system handles tickets for Shinkansen’s “Golden Route” and Kyushu.

If you’re planning to take a ride on the Shinkansen, the Smart EX online ticketing service is a handy utility. Managed by Shinkansen operator Central Japan Railway Company/JR Central, Smart EX lets you book seats on bullet trains running in eastern and western Japan, as well as the southwestern island of Kyushu. A wide selection of credit cards can be used for payment, and the Smart EX mobile app can provide you with a QR code so that you don’t have to fuss around with a paper ticket.

Unfortunately, it’s not just travelers that have found Smart EX alluring, but hackers too, as JR Central has announced a data breach has resulted in personal information of roughly 170,000 Smart EX users being leaked.

The incident stems from another security breach earlier this month at Yumirulink, a digital marketing and email forwarding service involved in the routing of some Smart EX messages.

Thankfully, the Smart EX user data that was stolen is of a limited scope. According to JR Central’s statement, hackers were able to obtain the users’ names, email addresses, member IDs/screen names, and membership types. Date of birth, home addresses, phone numbers, and credit card numbers and expiration dates were not leaked, the company says. In addition, JR Central says that only the renderings of users’ names in Japanese katakana phonetic characters were leaked, and other forms were not compromised. However, it’s somewhat unclear if this assertion applies only to non-katakana Japanese text (i.e. kanji-character) versions of user names, or if it also is meant to cover names written in the Latin alphabet, since as of this writing the Smart EX website only has a statement regarding the data leak on its Japanese-language page, with no mention of it on the service’s English site.

JR Central’s statement also says that the data breach was not connected to auto-generated emails such as those that Smart EX sends to confirm bookings or customer-initiated schedule changes, and instead is related to emails sent for things such as sale promotions or altered timetable notifications following the recent Kumamoto earthquake.

Collectively, the Smart EX system covers Shinkansen bookings for bullet trains operated by JR Central, JR West, and JR Kyushu, which together stretch from Tokyo through Osaka, Kyoto, and Hiroshima on to Fukuoka and then down to Kagoshima. So if you’ve used the service to book a Shinkansen ticket along that network, it’s probably a good idea to keep an eye on your various other online accounts in the coming days, just in case someone out there has some of your personal data.

Source: Smart EX, Chukyo TV via Yahoo! Japan News via Hachima Kiko, Nitele News

title: Japan’s super cute tanuki bread skips tricks, promises to be treat for your eyes and taste buds
description: You can trust this tanuki to be as sweet on the inside as it looks on the outside. In Japanese folklore, tanuki are tricksters. There’s nothing they love more than playing pranks on us unsuspecting humans, and that image of them even extends to Japanese cuisine. “Tanuki soba” and “tanuki udon” are styles of noodles […]
content:
You can trust this tanuki to be as sweet on the inside as it looks on the outside.

In Japanese folklore, tanuki are tricksters. There’s nothing they love more than playing pranks on us unsuspecting humans, and that image of them even extends to Japanese cuisine. “Tanuki soba” and “tanuki udon” are styles of noodles topped with tempura flakes only, because those crafty racoon dogs have tricked you by already eating the shrimp or veggies that would ordinarily be inside the tempura.

But at the same time, tanuki are really, really cute, and thankfully it’s this aspect that Japanese bakery Kimuraya has chosen to focus on for the treats that’ll be coming out of their ovens next month.

Called Tanuki-kun (-kun being a form of address in Japanese that’s friendlier and more familiar than -san), these baked goods are the polar opposite from tanuki soba/udon in terms of filling generosity. Inside the bun is a mixture of caramel cream and chocolate chips, promising a richly sweet and satisfying flavor profile with an interesting texture too.

On the outside, the tanuki’s facial features are made of chocolate, and the mask-like marking around its eyes, and part of its ears too, are rendered with a chocolate biscuit dough.

Kimuraya is a little on the premium-priced side for a Japanese bakery, and the 400-yen (US$2.50) Tanuki-kun is likewise a little more expensive than the average bakery treat, but with something that looks this delicious and adorable, we can make room in our snack budget. The Tanuki-kun goes on sale at Kimuraya bakeries from November 1, but can also be ordered through the Kimuraya online store as of October 28.

title: Japanese snack lovers may soon be spore-ting the latest crowdfunded confectionery tech
description: Play that fung-ky music. From creepy penguins hatching from eggs to flying balls of chaos, Japan likes to jump on the latest quirky trends, and if history is anything to go by, people will soon be putting fungi in their ears. If you have ever browsed the snack aisle of a Japanese convenience store, there’s […]
content:
Play that fung-ky music.

From creepy penguins hatching from eggs to flying balls of chaos, Japan likes to jump on the latest quirky trends, and if history is anything to go by, people will soon be putting fungi in their ears. If you have ever browsed the snack aisle of a Japanese convenience store, there’s a chance that you might have encountered Kinoko no Yama, bite-sized treats consisting of a crunchy biscuit stem topped with a chocolate mushroom cap. Now, imagine putting one in your ear.

Rather than being the latest dietary trend, or attempting to commune deeper with nature through the chocolate mycelia, what appears to be the start of a fungal colony growing out of your head is in fact the second-generation Kinoko no Yama Wireless Earphones Pro, a tech accessory that looks like you’re using actual confectionery as audio equipment.

The concept originally started as a playful visual joke on social media, but after an overwhelming response from netizens demanding to know where they could buy a pair, Kagomedia collaborated with Kinoko no Yama’s maker Meiji to turn them into a reality. The first batch of 3,500 units launched on the Japanese crowdfunding platform Makuake in early 2024 and famously sold out in a shocking ten minutes.

▼ Achieving 9,836 percent of its one million yen goal.

Two and a half years later, these chocolate earbuds are making a comeback from November 1, with a new revival project for the updated 2027 Pro model. If the campaign sees at least 1,000 people pledge that they want a pair, the second generation will officially go into production, but this time they will be made-to-order without a strict limit on quantities, so all those who want will be able to get their hands and ears on them.

Despite looking like a novelty gimmick, these earbuds pack some serious tech, with upgraded audio tuning and gold-plated touch sensors. The most ambitious feature though is the built-in AI simultaneous translation covering 144 global languages and dialects. So while you might look like you’re trying to store your snacks in your ears for later to onlookers, you could be able to understand nearly 150 languages in real time.

The case itself is designed to mirror the original snack box, complete with a pop-up tray where the two little mushrooms rest inside.

If you, like your 3,500 predecessors, want some fungi in your head, you’ll need to check out Makuake on November 1 at 12:00 p.m., where for the first 24 hours, the first 1,000 pairs of earphones will be sold at the same price as the first-generation (29,800 yen [US$188.96]). The next 2,000 pairs can be bought for 31,800 yen, and the following 2,000 for 33,000 yen. The last possible discount is for 3,000 pairs at 34,800 yen before each unit is sold for its regular price of 36,300 yen with no quantity limits as long as the order is placed before December 13, 2026, after which you will not be able to purchase these any more.

Whether you find the design quirky or strange, it’s a high-quality blend of everyday Japanese pop culture with high-tech innovation, so there’s no need to panic the next time you spot someone on the train with mushrooms sprouting from their ears.
